name: Modern Crop Husbandry: Maize, Rice, Cassava and Legumes
objectives: For a staple crop you will grow next season, choose a variety from your national research institute or variety list and name a registered source of certified seed or clean cuttings, checking the label, seal or source before you pay
Given a spacing and the size of your field, calculate the plant population per hectare and per acre and the seed or cuttings you need, showing each step of the working
For your chosen crop and planting date, schedule land preparation, planting, feeding and weeding on a dated calendar, with weeding inside the crop's critical early weeks

Given the signs on a sick plant or field, identify maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic, cassava brown streak or rice blast and choose the first response, matching each disease to the right first step
At the end of the season, judge when the crop is ready and calculate the yield per hectare and per acre from a weighed harvest, using the right area and showing your working

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a variety and buying certified seed
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a variety that suits your area and name a registered source of certified seed or clean cuttings.
This lesson builds toward: For a staple crop you will grow next season, you will choose a variety from your national research institute or variety list and name a registered source of certified seed or clean cuttings, checking the label, seal or source before you pay.
A variety is a type of the crop bred for certain traits: early or late maturity, drought tolerance, disease resistance, grain colour or cooking quality. National research institutes test and release varieties for each area: KALRO in Kenya, the Nigerian research institutes working with IITA, CSIR-Crops Research Institute in Ghana, and CNRA in Côte d'Ivoire. IITA works on cassava, maize, cowpea and soybean, and AfricaRice, based in Abidjan, on rice. Ask your extension officer which varieties are recommended for your area, rainfall and market.
Choose for your conditions: early-maturing varieties for short rains or dry areas, tolerant or resistant varieties where a disease is common (for example maize lethal necrosis or cassava brown streak), and what buyers want (white or yellow maize, parboiling rice, sweet or bitter cassava).
Certified seed is seed inspected by the national seed authority for purity and germination. In Kenya, KEPHIS certifies seed and publishes the National Crop Variety List, and certified packs carry a KEPHIS label you can verify. In Nigeria, the National Agricultural Seed Council (NASC) certifies seed. Buy sealed, labelled packs from a registered dealer. Hybrid maize seed must be bought new each season, because yield drops if you replant its grain. Open-pollinated varieties (OPV) and legumes can be saved for a few seasons if you select clean seed from healthy plants. For cassava, get clean cuttings from an inspected multiplier or a healthy field, never from a field with mosaic or brown streak. For soybean, ask about an inoculant (rhizobium) where extension advises it.
Step by step:
- Ask extension which varieties are recommended for your area and rainfall.
- Choose for maturity, disease resistance and what buyers want.
- Check the variety on the national list where one is published (for example KEPHIS in Kenya).
- Buy sealed, labelled, certified seed from a registered dealer; check the date and label.
- For cassava, get clean cuttings from an inspected multiplier or a healthy field.
Words to know:
- Variety: a type of a crop bred for certain traits, such as early maturity or disease resistance.
- Certified seed: seed checked by the national seed authority for purity and germination.
- Hybrid: seed from crossing two parent lines; it yields well but must be bought new each season.
- OPV: open-pollinated variety: seed that can be saved and replanted for a few seasons if kept clean.
- Inoculant: a product containing helpful bacteria that help legumes such as soybean fix nitrogen.
Official sources:
- Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS): seed certification and the National Crop Variety List
- National Agricultural Seed Council (NASC, Nigeria): seed certification
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
- International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA)
- AfricaRice (headquarters in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire)
Try it now: For one staple you will grow next season, ask your extension officer or agro-dealer for two recommended varieties. Write down their maturity, disease resistance and where you can buy certified seed or clean cuttings. If you are in Kenya, check the variety and dealer against KEPHIS's lists.
You can now choose a variety that suits your area and buy certified seed or clean cuttings from a registered source.

check.q: You planted hybrid maize last season. Can you replant the grain you harvested?
options: Yes, it will yield the same
Yes, if you plant it closer
No, yield drops; buy new certified hybrid seed
Only if you soak it in water
check.why: Hybrid seed loses its vigour in the next generation, so new seed is needed each season.

check.q: Your neighbour's cassava has yellow mosaic leaves. He offers you cuttings. What do you do?
options: Refuse and get clean cuttings from an inspected multiplier or healthy field
Take them and plant them near the road
check.why: Cassava viruses travel in cuttings, so sick fields spread the disease to yours.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Land preparation and plant population
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate plants per hectare and per acre from a spacing, and the seed or cuttings you need.
This lesson builds toward: Given a spacing and the size of your field, you will calculate the plant population per hectare and per acre and the seed or cuttings you need, showing each step of the working.
Prepare the land for the crop. Clear without burning, and keep residues as cover where you can. Maize, beans and groundnuts need a firm seedbed with fine soil around the seed; minimum tillage or planting basins work in many areas. Cassava in Nigeria and Ghana is often planted on ridges or mounds that drain well. Lowland rice needs bunds, a level field and good water control; transplanted rice is usually puddled.
Plant population is the number of plants per hectare. Too few plants waste land; too many compete for light, water and nutrients. Use the spacing your extension guide gives for your variety and area. To calculate: area for one plant = row spacing x plant spacing (in metres). Plants per hectare = 10,000 m2 / area per plant. Plants per acre = 4,047 m2 / area per plant (one acre is about 4,047 m2, and one hectare is about 2.47 acres).
Worked examples, if your guide gives these spacings: maize at 75 cm x 25 cm, one seed per hole: 0.75 x 0.25 = 0.1875 m2, so 10,000 / 0.1875 = about 53,300 plants per hectare, or 4,047 / 0.1875 = about 21,600 per acre. Cassava at 1 m x 1 m: 10,000 plants per hectare, about 4,000 per acre. Transplanted rice at 20 cm x 20 cm: 0.04 m2, so 250,000 hills per hectare. Beans at 50 cm x 10 cm: 0.05 m2, so 200,000 plants per hectare.
Seed needs: number of seeds / seeds per kg (count and weigh 100 seeds, or read the pack) = kg, plus about 10% for gaps. For cassava, count cuttings (often about 20 to 25 cm long, from mature stems), plus a few spares. Then fill gaps within a week or two of emergence.
Step by step:
- Measure your field in metres; area = length x width.
- Get the recommended spacing for your variety and area.
- Area per plant = row spacing x plant spacing (in metres).
- Plants per hectare = 10,000 / area per plant; per acre = 4,047 / area per plant.
- Plants on your field = field area / area per plant.
- Seed: plants / seeds per kg, plus about 10%.
Words to know:
- Plant population: the number of plants per hectare or per acre.
- Hectare (ha): an area of 10,000 square metres, about 2.47 acres.
- Acre: an area of about 4,047 square metres, about 0.4 hectare.
- Bund: a low earth wall around a rice field that holds water.
- Puddling: working wet soil in a rice field to make soft mud that holds water and controls weeds.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO)
- International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA)
Try it now: Measure one of your fields (or use its size in acres x 4,047 to get square metres). Get the spacing for your crop from extension, then calculate the plants per hectare, per acre and on your field, and how much seed or how many cuttings to buy.
You can now work out plant population per hectare and per acre from a spacing, and how much seed or how many cuttings you need.

check.q: Cassava is planted at 1 m x 1 m. How many plants per hectare?
check.why: Each plant uses 1 m2, and a hectare is 10,000 m2.

check.q: A field is 0.5 hectare and maize needs about 53,300 plants per hectare. About how many plants do you need?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Feeding and weeding on time
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Schedule planting, feeding and weeding on a dated calendar for your crop.
This lesson builds toward: For your chosen crop and planting date, you will schedule land preparation, planting, feeding and weeding on a dated calendar, with weeding inside the crop's critical early weeks.
Soil testing, manure, compost and fertilizer are taught in "Soil Health and Fertility"; use your soil test or your extension officer's advice for what and how much to apply. What changes by crop is when and what each one needs most. Maize is hungry for nitrogen and needs it early and again as it grows fast. Legumes (beans, cowpea, groundnuts, soybean) make much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so they need phosphorus more than nitrogen. Cassava grows on poorer soils but takes a lot of potassium from the soil over time. Rice usually gets nitrogen in split doses; too much nitrogen makes rice blast worse.
Weeds steal water, light and nutrients most in the first weeks after the crop comes up. This is the critical period: weeds then cost the most yield, and weeding later cannot win it back. Many guides give a first weeding about two to three weeks after the crop comes up and a second a few weeks later; check your local guide. Cassava grows slowly at first and needs to be kept clean for its first three months or so, until its leaves cover the ground. In lowland rice, good levelling and keeping water on the field help hold weeds down.
Herbicides can save labour but must be registered for your crop (PCPB in Kenya, NAFDAC in Nigeria) and used as the label says, with protective equipment. Put everything on a calendar counted from the planting date, so the work and the money are ready on time.
Step by step:
- Write your planting date.
- Add land preparation in the weeks before it.
- Add feeding as your soil test or extension advises, at the right crop stage.
- Add the first weeding inside the critical early weeks, and the next ones.
- Note when you need labour, inputs and money for each job.
Words to know:
- Critical period: the early weeks when weeds cause the most yield loss; weeding must happen then.
- Root nodules: small swellings on legume roots where bacteria turn nitrogen from the air into plant food.
- Split dose: giving fertilizer in two or more parts at different crop stages instead of all at once.
- Herbicide: a chemical that kills weeds; it must be registered and used as its label says.
Official sources:
- 4R Plant Nutrient Management in African Agriculture: an extension handbook for fertilizer management
- Pest Control Products Board (Kenya): registered products
- NAFDAC (Nigeria): registered agrochemicals
Try it now: Write a calendar for your crop starting from your planned planting date: land preparation, planting, each feeding your soil test or extension officer advises, and each weeding. Mark the critical weeding period in a different colour.
You can now plan feeding and weeding on a dated calendar so weeds are controlled in the critical early weeks.

check.q: When do weeds cause the most yield loss?
options: In the first weeks after the crop comes up
check.why: The critical period is the early weeks; later weeding cannot win that yield back.

check.q: Which crop makes much of its own nitrogen through root nodules?
check.why: Legumes such as beans fix nitrogen with the help of bacteria in their root nodules.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Key diseases: maize lethal necrosis, cassava viruses and rice blast
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic, cassava brown streak and rice blast and choose a first response.
This lesson builds toward: Given the signs on a sick plant or field, you will identify maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic, cassava brown streak or rice blast and choose the first response, matching each disease to the right first step.
Maize lethal necrosis (MLN) hit Kenya hard from 2011 and spread in East Africa. CIMMYT explains that it happens when maize is infected by two viruses together: maize chlorotic mottle virus and a potyvirus such as sugarcane mosaic virus. Leaves show yellow mottling, then dry from the edges inward; the centre of the plant can die, and cobs are small, empty or rotten. Insects such as thrips and aphids spread it in the field, and infected seed can carry it over long distances. Response: plant certified seed of MLN-tolerant varieties, rotate away from maize for a season with your neighbours, remove volunteer maize, control weeds, pull and destroy sick plants early, and report it to extension.
Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) makes leaves yellow-and-green patchy (mosaic), twisted and small, and stunts the plant. Cassava brown streak disease (CBSD) shows yellow patches along the veins of older leaves and brown streaks on stems, but the worst damage is hidden: the roots get a hard, brown, dry rot, sometimes when the leaves look almost healthy. IITA estimates these two diseases cost Africa about US$1 billion a year. Whiteflies spread both, but the main spread over long distances is farmers sharing infected cuttings. Response: plant clean cuttings of tolerant varieties, pull out and destroy sick plants early, never take cuttings from sick fields, and in East Africa dig a few roots to check for brown rot before harvest.
Rice blast is a fungal disease and a major problem in West Africa. On leaves it makes diamond- or eye-shaped spots with grey centres and brown edges. When it attacks the neck under the panicle, the panicle turns white and empty. Research with AfricaRice found that resistant varieties are the cheapest control for small farmers, but the fungus can overcome resistance a few years after a variety is widely grown, so new varieties matter. Response: grow a variety recommended as resistant, avoid too much nitrogen, avoid drought stress in upland rice, use clean seed and clear infected residues. Use a fungicide only if extension advises it and it is registered for rice.
Step by step:
- Scout weekly; compare what you see with the signs in this lesson.
- Photograph sick plants and ask extension or a plant clinic to confirm.
- Pull and destroy sick plants early (MLN and cassava viruses).
- Next season: certified seed or clean cuttings of a tolerant or resistant variety.
- Coordinate rotation and clean planting material with neighbours.
Words to know:
- MLN: maize lethal necrosis: a disease from two viruses together that can kill maize plants.
- CMD: cassava mosaic disease: a virus disease that makes cassava leaves patchy, twisted and small.
- CBSD: cassava brown streak disease: a virus disease that causes brown, dry rot in cassava roots.
- Rice blast: a fungal disease of rice that makes eye-shaped leaf spots and can leave panicles white and empty.
- Rogue: to pull out and destroy diseased plants so they do not spread disease.
Official sources:
- CIMMYT: Understanding and preventing seed transmission of maize lethal necrosis (MLN) in Africa
- IITA: Spirited effort by IITA team to manage the viruses destroying cassava in Africa (2017)
- JIRCAS with AfricaRice: Genetic variation of blast resistance in rice from West Africa (2017)
- AfricaRice (headquarters in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire)
Try it now: Walk your field (or a neighbour's) and look for the signs of the disease that matters most for your crop. Write what you saw, take a photo of anything doubtful, and write the first response you would take for that disease.
You can now recognize maize lethal necrosis, cassava mosaic, cassava brown streak and rice blast and choose a first response.

check.q: Your cassava leaves look almost healthy, but roots dug up show hard, brown, dry rot. The most likely cause is:
check.why: CBSD rots the roots, sometimes with only mild leaf signs.

check.q: Rice leaves have eye-shaped spots with grey centres and brown edges. What is a good response?
options: Plant the same seed again next season
Ask extension to confirm blast and grow a resistant variety next season
check.why: Those are blast spots; resistant varieties and balanced nitrogen are the main controls.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Knowing when to harvest
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Judge when your maize, rice, cassava or legume crop is ready to harvest.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of the season, you will judge when the crop is ready and calculate the yield per hectare and per acre from a weighed harvest, using the right area and showing your working.
Harvest too early and grain is light and wet; harvest too late and you lose crop to birds, rats, rain, shattering and rot, and grain is more likely to get aflatoxin. Drying and storage are taught in "Post-Harvest Handling and Storage".
Maize is mature when a black layer forms where the grain joins the cob and the husks are dry; pull back a few husks and break a few grains to check. Then dry it well before storing. Rice is ready when most of the grains on the panicles have turned golden and hard; waiting too long brings shattering and bird losses. Beans and cowpea are ready when most pods are dry and rattle; pick before they split. Groundnuts are ready when the leaves yellow and the inside of most shells has darkened; dig a few plants to check.
Cassava does not have one harvest day: each variety has a maturity period, and roots can stay in the ground for a while. But roots left too long can become woody, and where brown streak is common the rot gets worse. Once dug, cassava spoils within a few days, so harvest only what you can sell or process quickly. In Ghana and Nigeria, many farmers time the harvest with the gari or fufu processor's capacity.
Step by step:
- Know your variety's maturity period from the seed pack or extension.
- Check a few plants across the field, not just one.
- Maize: black layer and dry husks; rice: most grains golden and hard.
- Legumes: dry, rattling pods; groundnuts: darkened shell insides.
- Cassava: harvest only what you can sell or process within days.
Words to know:
- Black layer: a dark spot where a maize grain joins the cob; it shows the grain has stopped filling.
- Shattering: grain or pods falling or splitting open in the field before harvest.
- Maturity period: how long a variety takes from planting to harvest.
Try it now: For your crop, write the variety's maturity period, the signs you will check, and the date you expect to start checking. If your crop is in the field now, check five plants across the field and write what you see.
You can now judge when your staple crop is ready to harvest.

check.q: How do you know maize grain has stopped filling?
options: A black layer forms where the grain joins the cob
check.why: The black layer shows physiological maturity.

check.q: Why harvest only as much cassava as you can sell or process within a few days?
options: Cassava roots spoil quickly once dug
Cassava roots grow back after digging
check.why: Fresh cassava roots go bad within days of harvest.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Calculating yield and writing your production plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate yield per hectare and per acre and write a production plan for one staple on your field.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of the season, you will judge when the crop is ready and calculate the yield per hectare and per acre from a weighed harvest, using the right area and showing your working. Given a spacing and the size of your field, you will calculate the plant population per hectare and per acre and the seed or cuttings you need, showing each step of the working. For your chosen crop and planting date, you will schedule land preparation, planting, feeding and weeding on a dated calendar, with weeding inside the crop's critical early weeks.
Yield is the weight of crop you harvest per area. To know it, weigh your harvest after drying, and know the exact area it came from. Yield per hectare = kg harvested / area in m2 x 10,000. Yield per acre = kg harvested / area in m2 x 4,047. Or from per hectare to per acre: divide by 2.47.
Example, maize in Kenya: you harvest 1,350 kg of dry grain from a field of 3,000 m2. Per hectare: 1,350 / 3,000 x 10,000 = 4,500 kg, or 4.5 tonnes. Per acre: 4,500 / 2.47 = about 1,820 kg, which is about 20 bags of 90 kg. A quick estimate before harvest: mark a 10 m x 10 m square (100 m2) in a typical part of the field, harvest and dry it, weigh it, and multiply by 100 to get kg per hectare. Do it in two or three places and take the average.
Now put the whole course together into a production plan for one staple on your own field: the field size, the variety and seed source, the spacing with your plant population and seed needs, a dated calendar for land preparation, planting, feeding and weeding, the main diseases and your first response, how you will judge harvest, and a yield target per hectare and per acre. After harvest, compare the real yield with your target and write what you will change. A farmer in Côte d'Ivoire who writes down her rice yield every season can show a buyer, a cooperative or a lender what her field produces.
Step by step:
- Measure the area harvested in m2.
- Weigh the dried harvest in kg.
- Per hectare = kg / m2 x 10,000; per acre = kg / m2 x 4,047.
- Or sample 100 m2 in 2 or 3 spots, weigh and multiply by 100 for kg/ha.
- Write the plan: variety, seed, population, calendar, diseases, harvest, yield target.
- After harvest, compare real yield with the target.
Words to know:
- Yield: the amount of crop harvested per area, such as kg per hectare or bags per acre.
- Tonne: 1,000 kilograms.
- Sample plot: a small marked area harvested and weighed to estimate the yield of the whole field.
Try it now: Final task: write your crop production plan for one staple on your own field: field size in hectares and acres, variety and seed source, spacing with plant population and seed needs worked out, a dated calendar (land preparation, planting, feeding, weeding), the two main diseases and your first response to each, harvest signs, and a yield target per hectare and per acre with your working.
You can now calculate yield per hectare and per acre and write a production plan for one staple on your own field.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Variety and seed No variety named, or seed is recycled hybrid grain or cuttings from a sick field. A recommended variety for the area is named, with a registered source of certified seed or clean cuttings. Two varieties are compared on maturity, disease resistance and market, and the choice is explained. Plant population and seed needs No spacing or calculation, or the arithmetic is wrong. The spacing, plants per hectare, per acre and on the field, and the seed or cuttings needed are worked out correctly with the steps shown. Also plans gap filling and a count of plants after emergence to check the real population. Dated calendar Jobs are listed without dates, or weeding is late. Land preparation, planting, feeding (from a soil test or extension) and each weeding are dated from the planting date, with the first weeding inside the critical period. Labour, inputs and cash needed for each job are on the calendar. Disease watch No diseases named, or the responses do not fit them. The two main diseases for the crop are named with their signs and a correct first response for each. Includes prevention for next season agreed with neighbours, such as rotation or clean planting material. Harvest and yield target No harvest signs or yield target, or the yield maths is wrong. Harvest signs for the crop and a yield target per hectare and per acre with correct working. Includes a sample-plot method to estimate yield before harvest and a plan to compare the result with the target. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again with your extension officer.

check.q: You harvested 900 kg of dry beans from 4,047 m2. What is the yield per acre?
check.why: 4,047 m2 is one acre, so the yield is 900 kg per acre.

check.q: A 100 m2 sample plot gives 40 kg of dry maize. What is the estimated yield per hectare?
check.why: A hectare is 100 times 100 m2, so 40 x 100 = 4,000 kg per hectare.
